blocks.text: A string is "good" if there are no repeated characters in it. Given a string s, return the number of good substrings of length 3 in s.

blocks.text: A string is "good" if it has no repeated characters. Given a string s, return the number of good substrings of length exactly 3.

If s has fewer than 3 characters, there are no length-3 substrings at all, so the answer is 0.

Before rebuilding a fresh set for every window, notice this is the exact same fixed-size sliding window shape used in Maximum Sum of Distinct Subarrays With Length K, just with a fixed window size of 3.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: This is a fixed-size sliding window (size 3), the same shape used whenever a problem asks about every window of a specific length.

Observation 2: A window is "good" exactly when all of its characters are distinct, meaning the number of DISTINCT characters inside it equals its own size, 3.

Observation 3: Maintain a frequency map of characters currently in the window, updated the same way the window itself slides: add the entering character's count, remove the leaving character's count once it reaches 0.

Observation 4: At every fully-formed window, check whether the frequency map's size (its distinct-character count) equals 3; if so, this window is good, and the counter increments.

Maintaining a frequency map alongside a sliding window turns a validity check that would otherwise need rebuilding a fresh set every time into an O(1) size comparison per slide.

This is a direct, smaller-scale application of the same technique used for finding the best sum among distinct-element windows, just counting how many windows qualify instead of tracking a maximum sum.
For every possible length-3 window, build a fresh set of its characters and check whether all three are distinct.

items: Loop over every valid starting position for a length-3 window.
For each window, build a set of its 3 characters, and count it as good if the set has all 3 distinct entries.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: A fresh set is built for every window, since each window's distinctness needs to be checked independently.
The window size (3) is small and fixed, so building a tiny set for each window is cheap per window, even though it repeats work across overlapping windows.
The count only increments when the set's size matches exactly 3, meaning all three characters are genuinely different.

blocks.text: Every window's true distinctness is checked directly, so the correct count is always found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n) overall, since the window size (3) is a small constant, making each window check O(1); this is already efficient given the fixed window size, but the underlying idea still rebuilds state per window.
Space: O(1) extra, since each temporary set holds at most 3 entries.

Limitation: even though the constant window size keeps this brute force fast in practice, rebuilding a fresh set for every window still repeats work that could instead be maintained incrementally, and does not generalize if the window size were larger or variable.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force rebuilds a fresh set for every single window, discarding all state between neighboring windows even though they share 2 of their 3 characters. Instead, maintain a frequency map of characters currently in the window, updated incrementally as the window slides: add the entering character, remove the leaving character once its count reaches 0. A window is good exactly when the frequency map's size (its distinct-character count) equals 3, turning the validity check into an O(1) size comparison rather than a fresh set rebuild.

Slide a window of size 3 across s, maintaining a frequency map of characters currently in the window. At every fully-formed window, check whether the frequency map has exactly 3 distinct keys; if so, increment the count of good substrings.
Maintain a frequency map incrementally as the window slides, checking its distinct-character count at each fully-formed window.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single pass.
Space: O(1) extra, since the frequency map holds at most 3 entries (the lowercase alphabet bounds it further, but the window itself already caps it at 3).

The frequency map tracks exactly how many times each character currently appears within the window. Its size (the number of distinct keys) can never exceed the window's length, 3, and it equals 3 precisely when every character in the window is different, since a repeated character would collapse two positions onto the same key, reducing the distinct count below 3.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Distinct count","Meaning"],"rows":[["Distinct count equals 3","All three characters in the window are different","The window is good, increment the count"],["Distinct count is less than 3","At least one character repeats within the window","The window is not good, skip it"]]}

items: The frequency map is updated every time the window slides: the entering character's count increases, and the leaving character's count decreases (and is removed entirely once it reaches 0).
The validity check (distinct count equals 3) only happens once the window has reached its full size, guarded by the index check.
Because the window size is a small fixed constant, the frequency map never holds more than 3 entries at any point.

blocks.text: Even though the fixed, tiny window size (3) makes the brute force already fast here, maintaining a frequency map incrementally is the technique that generalizes to larger window sizes and to problems like Maximum Sum of Distinct Subarrays With Length K.

items: Leaving a character in the frequency map with a count of 0 instead of removing it entirely, which would incorrectly inflate the distinct-count check.
Checking window validity before the window has actually reached its full size of 3 characters, producing false results on partially-formed windows.
Confusing this fixed window-size-of-3 problem with a general k-sized version, forgetting that the constant here is baked directly into the problem, not a parameter.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["s has fewer than 3 characters","There are no length-3 windows at all, so the count is 0"],["s consists of only one repeated character","No window can ever have 3 distinct characters, so the count is 0"]]}

items: Point out explicitly that this is a smaller-scale version of the general "distinct-elements sliding window" pattern, with the window size fixed at exactly 3 by the problem itself.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Count how many FIXED-size windows have no repeated elements" points toward a frequency map maintained alongside a sliding window, checking distinct-count equals window size at each step.

items: How would this generalize to counting good substrings of an arbitrary length k, not just 3? The exact same frequency map technique applies directly, just with the window size and validity threshold both set to k instead of 3.

What if you needed to also list the actual substrings, not just count them? Append the current window's substring to a result list every time it is found to be good, alongside incrementing the counter.

How would you count good substrings across multiple different strings efficiently? The same single-pass technique would simply be repeated once per string, since each string is processed independently.
A smaller-scale, fixed-window-size-3 version of the same "frequency map for distinct-count validity" technique used in Maximum Sum of Distinct Subarrays With Length K.
Shares its fixed-size sliding window foundation with Maximum Average Subarray I and Maximum Number of Vowels in a Substring of Given Length.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n) time (due to the constant window size), O(1) space.
Optimized (incremental frequency map): O(n) time, O(1) space.

items: Pattern: Fixed-size (size 3) sliding window with an incrementally-maintained frequency map for distinct-character detection
Core Idea: A window is good exactly when its frequency map's distinct-character count equals the window size, 3
Time: O(n)
Space: O(1)
Most Important Observation: This is a smaller, fixed-size-3 instance of the general "distinct elements in a sliding window" pattern
Interview Difficulty: Easy
One-line memory trick: Slide the frequency map along with the window; good exactly when distinct count hits 3
